summary:
North Korea exposes trans visitors to unbounded official discretion rather than to a defined offence. The Criminal Code of 1950, revised in 2009, appears to contain no penalty for consensual same-sex acts, but Article 193 prohibits the import, possession and distribution of "decadent culture," including sexual recordings, and Article 262 punishes collective "obscene activities." Neither provision is defined in terms that constrain how the authorities apply it.

The US State Department's 2022 human rights report on North Korea reaches the same position: no specific law criminalises same-sex conduct, and the regime's total control leaves no space for LGBT life. Its 2020 report states that reliable information on LGBT persons is unavailable and that repression of all civil society is the dominant human-rights reality in the country.

Gender identity has no standing in the legal order. The Constitution, last revised in 2024, does not address discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no provision of North Korean law prohibits such discrimination; the US State Department reports that the concepts do not appear in the country's legal texts. As of 2026 no law recognises same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships. Article 8 of the Family Law of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea states that marriage may be concluded only between one man and one woman.

Official hostility is documented on the state record even while the state denies the existence of homosexuality. A KCNA commentary of 22 April 2014 rejected the UN Commission of Inquiry's report on North Korean human rights as a political fabrication and personally attacked commissioner Michael Kirby as "a disgusting old lecher with a 40-odd-year-long career of homosexuality" in order to discredit the findings. KCNA had denied homosexuality's existence earlier the same year.

Violence against LGBT people is reported but thinly sourced. A 2023 South Korean Ministry of Unification report, the 584-page North Korean Human Rights Report, cites defector testimony alleging that at least one male detainee in a detention camp was secretly executed for homosexuality in 2014. A 2011 Korea Times report, sourced to Free North Korea Radio, claimed that North Korea executed a lesbian couple, a North Korean woman and a Japanese woman, for capitalist influence and "corruption of public morals." Outright International's country page records no documented state or non-state violence against LGBTIQ people, which reflects the absence of reporting channels rather than an absence of incidents.

Exit narratives form the main body of evidence. An openly gay defector published an autobiography in 2017, and CNN's April 2017 account of that defector records both the place of homosexuality in North Korean society and the punishment it carries. Jang Young-jin, a novelist who fled in the late 1990s and was forcibly outed, is documented by BBC Korean in October 2024 as the first publicly known gay defector; the same feature describes how a regime subordinating the individual to the collective forces sexual minorities into silent self-suppression.

The legislative environment has tightened. BBC Korean's 10 October 2024 feature, produced ten years after the UN Commission of Inquiry report, identifies new laws including the Pyongyang Cultural Protection Act as extending state control over expression. Article 193's ban on decadent material and Article 262's ban on collective obscene activities sit within this framework, and neither carries a defined penalty range in the sources reviewed.
tangentialFactors:
The evidentiary base for North Korea is dominated by defector testimony and foreign government reporting, which means allegations of execution or punishment are difficult to corroborate independently. The 2011 lesbian-couple execution claim rests on a single radio source, and the 2014 camp execution allegation is presented as testimony rather than as a verified finding.

Official rhetoric is a risk factor in its own right. The state news agency's 2014 attack on a UN commissioner used homosexuality as an insult, which indicates that visible association with LGBT identity can be framed as disqualifying or politically hostile by the authorities, independently of any statute.

Outright International's position that no state or non-state violence against LGBTIQ people is documented sits alongside the Ministry of Unification's execution allegations. The apparent contradiction is best read as a measure of how little independent reporting leaves the country, not as confirmation that violence does not occur.

The absence of a criminalisation statute does not produce a permissive environment. Comparable jurisdictions in the region combine decodified or unenforced sodomy provisions with sweeping public-order and national-security offences, and North Korea's Articles 193 and 262 function in that same discretionary space.

The UN Commission of Inquiry's 2014 findings remain the reference point for international assessments of the country, and the regime's rebuttal of that report has been consistently personal and derogatory rather than substantive.
localsOnly:
Changing the sex marker on a birth certificate or citizen card is technically possible under "unavoidable circumstances." The application goes to the People's Security Agency and requires a state forensic medical evaluation, and in practice the route requires surgical intervention.

No law explicitly bans gender-affirming care, but the under-resourced health system makes hormones and surgery effectively inaccessible to residents.

Same-sex couples cannot legally adopt children, per the US State Department's 2020 report. Marriage is limited by Article 8 of the Family Law to one man and one woman, and no recognition mechanism exists for same-sex unions of any kind.

No registration route exists for LGBTI organisations, and the United States Department of State states that no provisions in North Korean law prohibit discrimination on sexual orientation or identity.

The collective-over-individual structure of the state pushes sexual minorities into silent self-suppression; the few who have gone public, such as the novelist Jang Young-jin, did so only after leaving the country, and defectors who have come out openly have faced exposure against their will.
outOfScopeNotes:
Entry and border-screening practice for trans travellers, including how immigration officers treat foreign passport gender markers, is not addressed by any source in this inventory and remains unresolved here.

The claim that the Criminal Code contains no penalty for consensual same-sex acts is phrased in the source as an apparent absence rather than an affirmative verification; a definitive reading of the 2009 revised text is not available from these materials.

Whether Articles 193 and 262 have been applied to consensual same-sex conduct specifically is not sourced. Their use in any individual case is unresolved.

The execution allegations from 2011 and 2014 are unverified by any source in this inventory; no corroborating record, name or case file is available.

Access to legal redress for a foreign visitor who experiences violence is not covered by these sources. No consular, complaint or protection mechanism for trans visitors is documented here.
